694.title: Your own feast days
694.hook: many Catholics keep their baptism day and their saint's name day
694.howItsDone: In many Catholic countries people celebrate the feast of the saint whose name they bear, with greetings, cake or a small gift, and some families also mark each child's baptism anniversary, sometimes by lighting the baptismal candle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day, Dominica, the first day of a new creation. Your line was a little easter.

In a Polish office in late July, someone walks in with a box of pastries, and the whole floor sings to Anna. It isn't her birthday; nobody there knows her birthday. It's the feast of Saint Anne, and so it's her imieniny, her name day. Orthodox neighbors in Greece keep it too: the same thing can happen to a Giorgos on Saint George's day, and the phone doesn't stop ringing. The calendar of saints walked all year isn't only the Church's calendar. In some places, it's personal.
screen: `PASTRIES FOR ANNA.` → `NOT HER BIRTHDAY.` → `A CALENDAR THAT GETS PERSONAL.`

segments.voice: A name day is the feast of the saint whose name you carry. By long custom, Catholic children were given a saint's name at baptism, and that saint became their patron: a friend in heaven, an example, someone to ask for prayers. Church law still asks parents, godparents and the pastor not to give a name foreign to Christian sense, though it doesn't require a saint's name. The Catechism, in paraphrase, says that in baptism the Lord's name sanctifies a person, and a Christian receives his or her own name in the Church. Behind that is an old line from Isaiah, where God says to his people, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have redeemed thee, and called thee by thy name: thou art mine." In some Catholic countries the name day is still a real celebration: Italians call it the onomastico; Poles, imieniny. Some Catholics keep a second feast: the day of their baptism. At his general audiences, Pope Francis asked people whether they knew the date of their own baptism, and suggested they find out and celebrate it like a birthday, because for Catholics that day is a kind of birth. Some families light the baptismal candle again each year. And if your name isn't a saint's name? Catholics may take a saint's name at confirmation. Others look for a saint from their town, or one who shared their work, or whose feast falls on their birthday. The point isn't the name itself. It's that the great calendar of the Church has one day in it marked with your name.

segments.voice: Say your own first name slowly in your head, and ask whether a saint carries it, or something close. If you know, picture that person, where they lived and what they're remembered for; if you don't, hold the question of whose name you carry, and, if you're baptized, the date it happened. If you pray, ask your saint to pray for you.

695.title: The three-year cycle
695.hook: Sundays read Matthew, then Mark, then Luke, with John in Lent and Easter
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the book is a person
695.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass Catholics hear an Old Testament reading, a Psalm, a reading from the letters and a Gospel set by the lectionary's three-year cycle; many missals and apps show the year's letter and the readings for each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name day, the feast of the saint whose name you carry. Your line was your own feast.

Go to Mass in Chicago one Sunday, then fly to Manila and go again the next. The language changes, but the Gospel in Manila picks up right where Chicago's left off, because both parishes are reading from the same plan. Keep going every Sunday for three years and you'll hear Matthew, Mark and Luke in turn, without anyone choosing a passage on the day. Sunday missals mark the plan with a single capital letter that tells you where you are.
screen: `CHICAGO, THEN MANILA.` → `ONE PLAN, ANOTHER LANGUAGE.` → `ONE CAPITAL LETTER.`

segments.voice: The Second Vatican Council asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up more lavishly, so that people would hear a fuller share of scripture over a set number of years. The answer was a new lectionary, the book of readings, issued in 1969. Before it, the Sunday readings came round the same way each year; the new one spread the Sunday Gospels over three years. Year A reads Matthew, Year B reads Mark, Year C reads Luke. John has no year of his own, because he gets the great seasons: much of Lent and Easter in every year, and in Year B, which is short because Mark is short, a run of summer Sundays from John chapter six, the bread of life. Each Sunday also has an Old Testament reading chosen to echo the Gospel, a Psalm, and a reading from the letters. The weekdays run on a separate two-year cycle for the first reading. The cycle turns over on the First Sunday of Advent, not on New Year's Day. The trick for finding the letter: take the calendar year in which the Church's year ends and divide it by three. No remainder means Year C, a remainder of one means A, two means B. So the year that ends in November 2026 is Year A, Matthew, and Advent 2026 begins Year B. It reached beyond Catholic churches too: some Protestant churches use the Revised Common Lectionary, which grew out of it, so neighbors down the street may hear the same Gospel on a given Sunday. And this is the last day of the year of feasts.

segments.voice: Take the year the Church's current year ends in and divide it by three in your head; take your time. When you've got the letter, think of its Gospel and one story from it you remember from these two years, a parable, a healing, a meal, and hold that scene as if you were hearing it read aloud on Sunday.

696.title: Year two close: the book is a person
696.hook: a whole Bible in order, and the Church's year; Catholics say every page points to Christ
696.tomorrow: Year three opens: the story after Acts
696.howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole sweep of scripture read at Mass through the Church's year, and the Church encourages personal reading too, often slowly, as in lectio divina, with the Gospels at the center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three-year cycle and its lectio. Your line was a, b, c. Today, the last day of year two.

On the evening of the first Easter, two disciples are walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs, Luke says, of dust and disappointment. A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about. They tell him everything: the hopes, the cross, the strange report of an empty tomb. And the stranger, instead of comforting them, starts at the beginning of their own scriptures and walks them through it, Moses and the prophets, mile after mile. Later they'll say their hearts were burning.
screen: `THE ROAD TO EMMAUS.` → `A STRANGER WALKS BESIDE THEM.` → `MOSES AND THE PROPHETS, MILE AFTER MILE.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them in all the scriptures, the things that were concerning him." Catholics take that verse as the key to reading the whole Bible, and it's the road this year has walked. First, the beginning: Genesis, a garden, a flood, Abraham's tent, Joseph forgiving his brothers; then out of Egypt, the sea, the mountain, the law; then the kings, the prophets, the wisdom books, and the seven books found in Catholic Bibles, from Tobit to the Maccabees. Second, the Gospels: Luke's mercy, then John's signs and his Word made flesh. Third, the Church on the move: Acts, Paul's letters from Romans to Philemon, Hebrews and James, Peter, John and Jude, and the Apocalypse with its new heaven and new earth. Fourth, the year of feasts, from Advent to Christ the King, and this last week: Friday, Saturday, Sunday and your own name. Saint Augustine put that reading in a pair of lines: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, said it more sharply: not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ. For Catholics, the Bible isn't finally a book of rules or a book of history, though it holds both. It's a long way of meeting someone. And on that road, the disciples knew the stranger at last when he broke the bread. Tomorrow, year three: the story after Acts, the long history of the Church.

segments.voice: Let this year's books pass by as they come: a garden, a burning bush, a psalm, a prodigal son walking home, a Samaritan woman at a well, a shipwreck, a letter, a city coming down from heaven. Notice which one tugs at you, and don't argue with it; that's the book you keep, a few verses at a time. If you pray, ask to recognize him in it.

697.title: Year three opens: the story after Acts
697.hook: the Church keeps its history honestly: holiness and failure side by side
697.howItsDone: Catholics learn the Church's history through the saints of the calendar, parish and family stories, and the Church's own teaching, which calls the Church holy while saying its members always need purifying and forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emmaus, and year two's close: every page pointing to Christ. Your line was the book is a person.

The Acts of the Apostles ends in a rented room in Rome. Paul is under guard, waiting for his case to be heard. He stays two whole years, welcoming everyone who comes, preaching without anyone stopping him. Then the book simply stops. No verdict. No trial. Not a word about how Paul dies, or Peter either. The Bible's story of the Church breaks off with a door open and visitors still coming in. Year three walks through that door.
screen: `A RENTED ROOM IN ROME.` → `NO VERDICT, NO TRIAL.` → `THE BOOK SIMPLY STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here are the last words of Acts, in the Douay-Rheims: "Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition." After that, the record passes to other hands: letters, martyrs' stories, sermons, councils. That long record is church history, and this year walks through it in order. First, the Gospels themselves don't hide the first disciples' failures. Peter, the rock, denies Jesus by a charcoal fire. The others scatter. Paul admits he once hunted Christians down. So the story after them was never going to be clean. Second, a parable from Matthew: the wheat and the cockle. A man sows good seed, an enemy sows weeds in the night, and the servants want to rip them out. The master says, in the Douay, "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." Saint Augustine read that field as the Church in this age: good and bad in the same soil, sorted only at the end. Third, the year ahead. You'll meet martyrs who forgave the crowds that killed them, monks who fed the hungry, and a woman who told a pope to go home to Rome. You'll also meet crusades, inquisitions, corrupt bishops, and the wounds of abuse. Catholic teaching calls the Church holy because of Christ, and says plainly it is always in need of being purified, because its members sin. A pope in our own times publicly asked forgiveness for wrongs done by Christians. Fourth, why tell it this way. A history with only saints would be a statue, not a family. Honest history lets holiness show against the real background, and leaves room for ordinary people: a bit of both.
screen: `THE GOSPELS DON'T HIDE FAILURE.` · `THE WHEAT AND THE COCKLE.` · `MARTYRS AND CRUSADES, BOTH AHEAD.` · `A FAMILY, NOT A STATUE.` · then, large: `SUFFER BOTH TO GROW UNTIL THE HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Go back through your family's faith as far as you can: a parent, a grandparent, a half-remembered name. Who prayed, who stopped, who kept a rosary in a drawer or walked away and came back? Let the good and the hard sit side by side; if your family has no faith story, remember whoever first showed you kindness, and if you pray, name them before God.

698.title: Peter and Paul in Rome (c. 64–67)
698.hook: tradition holds Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded under Nero
698.howItsDone: Catholics keep one shared feast for Saints Peter and Paul, pray at the tombs tradition names as theirs in Rome, and pray for persecuted Christians at Mass and in their own prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, church history: Acts stops in Rome, and the long record begins. Your line was saints and sinners, both.

By the Sea of Tiberias, after a breakfast of bread and fish, the risen Jesus tells Peter how his life will end. When you were younger, he says, you dressed yourself and walked where you liked. When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and lead you where you would not go. John adds one quiet line: this was to show by what death Peter would glorify God. Then the Bible goes silent. Where Peter's road ends, and Paul's, is told by the generations after.
screen: `BY THE SEA OF TIBERIAS.` → `YOU WILL STRETCH OUT YOUR HANDS.` → `THE BIBLE GOES SILENT.`

segments.voice: Start with Paul. In the Second Letter to Timothy, Paul writes as a prisoner to a younger friend, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." A few lines later he asks Timothy to hurry before winter, and bring the cloak he left behind, and his books. A man who knows the end is close. Now the tradition. Early Christian writers, collected by the historian Eusebius, say both apostles died in Rome under the emperor Nero. Tradition says Paul, a Roman citizen as Acts tells us, was beheaded. And it says Peter was crucified, and asked to hang head downward, because he did not think himself worthy to die the way his Lord had. That detail comes from writings outside the Bible; Catholics hold it as tradition, not scripture. Now the names. In Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new one: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church." Catholics see the bishops of Rome as Peter's successors, and Saint Peter's Basilica stands over the place tradition names as his grave. The tentmaker: Acts says Paul made tents with his hands, and Paul writes that he labored night and day so as not to be a burden. A fisherman and a craftsman, and not always at peace: Paul says he opposed Peter to his face in Antioch over who could eat with whom. Yet the Church keeps their feast together, on one day. Some paintings set them side by side, Peter with the keys, Paul with the sword that tradition says took his head, and between them a quarrel neither the Bible nor the Church ever hid.

You don't need names: just someone, somewhere, who will go to Mass this week knowing it could cost them a job, a home, their safety. 699.title: Nero's fire
699.hook: Christians were blamed for the fire of Rome and killed as entertainment
699.howItsDone: The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, killed under Nero, and Catholics often pray for persecuted people at Mass in the prayers of the faithful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cephas: Peter the rock and Paul the tentmaker, two men, one feast. Your line was the rock and the tentmaker.

The man who tells this story didn't like Christians. Tacitus was a Roman senator and historian, and he called their faith a harmful superstition. Yet his history of the emperors is where their story survives. A fire broke out in Rome and raged through the city, burning whole districts. Afterward a rumor would not die: that the emperor Nero had wanted the fire. Relief for the homeless didn't stop it. Prayers to the gods didn't stop it. Nero needed somebody else to blame.
screen: `A HISTORIAN WHO DIDN'T LIKE THEM.` → `ROME BURNS.` → `A RUMOR THAT WON'T DIE.`

segments.voice: In his Annals, Tacitus says what happened next. To get rid of the rumor, Nero fastened the guilt on a group the crowd already hated, people called Christians. Tacitus even explains the name: it came from Christus, executed under Tiberius by the governor Pontius Pilate. First, the arrests. Those who confessed were taken first. Then, on what they disclosed, a great crowd of others, convicted, Tacitus says, not so much of setting the fire as of hatred of the human race. Second, the killing was a show. Some were dressed in animal skins and torn apart by dogs. Some were nailed to crosses. Some were set alight to serve as torches when daylight was gone. Nero opened his own gardens for it and mingled with the crowd. Third, a turn from the man who disliked them. Tacitus still calls them guilty, deserving the harshest punishment. Yet he writes that pity rose for them, because they were destroyed not for the public good, but to feed one man's cruelty. Fourth, what the Church remembers. Nobody knows these martyrs' names. The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for them anyway, the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, placed beside the feast of Peter and Paul. Their story echoes a line from the First Letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name." Scapegoating didn't end in Rome. When a city is afraid, a crowd still looks for someone to carry the fear: a minority, a newcomer, a neighbor who is different. Remembering these Christians makes it easier to see when it happens to anyone.

700.howItsDone: Some Catholics wear or display the fish as a sign of faith, and the early Christian paintings of fish and bread in the Roman catacombs can still be visited today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nero's fire, and nameless Christians made to carry a city's blame. Your line was blamed for the fire.

Two curved lines, crossing at one end to make a tail. It's on the backs of cars, on necklaces, on the sign of a plumber who wants you to know something about him. Now go underground, into the tunnels outside the walls of ancient Rome, where Christians buried their dead. On the plaster, by lamplight, the same creature shows up: a fish, sometimes swimming beside a basket of bread. Today's word is that fish, and it's hiding a sentence.
screen: `TWO CURVED LINES.` → `TUNNELS OUTSIDE ROME.` → `A FISH BESIDE THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: The Greek word for fish is ichthys. Spell it in Greek capitals and each letter starts a word: Iesous, Jesus. Christos, Christ. Theou, of God. Huios, Son. Soter, Savior. A whole creed, folded into one small animal. Saint Augustine explained it in The City of God, so by his time the word game was known. Second, why a fish fit so well. The Gospels are full of them. Jesus calls fishermen from their boats, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men." He feeds a crowd with loaves and a few fish. Third, the water. The writer Tertullian called Christians little fishes, born in water after the example of their Fish, Jesus Christ. He meant baptism: born in water, and like fish, kept alive by staying in it. Fourth, the catacombs. Films sometimes show Christians living down there in hiding. They were cemeteries: long tunnels of graves, where families came to bury and to pray, and where painters put their hope on the walls. Some read the fish beside the bread as a picture of the Eucharist. And the secret sign? A story people tell says one Christian would draw half a fish in the dirt, and a stranger who finished it was a friend. That story is hard to trace to any early writer. But the fish did work as a secret sign in a deeper way. To an outsider, it was only a fish. To someone who knew the letters, it was a confession of faith, hidden in plain sight.
